opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth separating two questions that often get blurred together. One is whether there's some chance that transformative AI arrives very soon, within months rather than years. The other is how we should act given that chance.

On the first, I'd say the probability is low but not negligible, and that's itself a remarkable thing to be able to say. Ten or fifteen years ago, almost no serious researcher would have put meaningful weight on that. Now you have people at the leading labs who openly talk about very short timelines, and while you should discount for the incentives and the enthusiasm of people close to the work, you also shouldn't dismiss them, because they see things the rest of us don't.

When I try to assess it myself, I look less at headline benchmark results, which can be gamed or can saturate in ways that overstate progress, and more at the underlying drivers. How much compute is going in, how quickly it's scaling, and whether we're getting returns that are holding up or starting to taper. In some areas, especially pre-training, there are signs the returns are less dramatic than people hoped. More of the recent progress has come from spending compute at inference time, letting models think longer, and from reinforcement learning on top. That's real progress, but it has a different cost structure. If you have to pay a lot more every time you use the model, that slows how fast capabilities can spread through the economy, even if the frontier is moving.

So my overall view is that the most likely picture is a matter of years, not months, with a lot of uncertainty in both directions. But I don't think the right response to a small probability of something very fast is to ignore it. If there's even a few percent chance that we're close, and that the transition could go badly, that's enormous in expected terms. It means some people, and some institutions, should be preparing as though it could happen soon: having governance mechanisms ready, having monitoring in place, thinking through what you'd actually do in the first weeks if it became clear a system had crossed some important threshold.

What I'd caution against is a kind of whiplash, where people swing between thinking it's imminent and thinking it's all hype depending on the latest news cycle. Better to hold a stable, calibrated distribution, update it gradually on real evidence, and build a portfolio of responses that makes sense across the range of timelines rather than betting everything on one.

r001.rationale: The response says years are more likely than months but that a small chance still warrants preparation; it does not state that long timelines do little to reduce concern about short timelines.

r002.rationale: It discusses scaling compute and inference-time progress, but does not identify explosive capability growth as a possible consequence of incremental improvements to existing architectures.

r003.rationale: The response does not say Toby Ord cannot rule out advanced AI already having been developed secretly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "within months" is a very strong claim, and I'd want to be careful about what we actually mean by it. If we mean something like a system that can do essentially everything a skilled human can do at a computer, and do it reliably, then I'd put quite a low probability on that arriving in the next few months. Not zero, but low. The systems we have are remarkable, and they keep surprising people, but there's still a real gap between impressive demonstrations and the kind of robust, sustained, autonomous competence that would mark a genuine transition.

That said, I don't think the right response to that low probability is to dismiss it. A few percent chance of something that would reshape the world is still enormously important. If you told me there was a few percent chance of a major war breaking out in the next few months, nobody would say that was too small to think about. So I'd separate two questions: what's most likely, and what deserves our attention. Short timelines deserve attention even if they're not the modal outcome.

The other thing I'd say is that the uncertainty itself is the striking feature here. A decade ago, if you asked serious researchers about timelines, you'd get answers spread over many decades, with a lot of weight on "maybe never." Now you have thoughtful people seriously arguing about whether it's two years or ten. The distribution has compressed dramatically, and its centre has moved a lot closer. That shift is the real story, more than any particular point estimate.

So my honest answer is: I'd be surprised if it arrived within months, but I'd be far less surprised than I would have been five years ago, and I think we're badly underprepared for even the scenarios I consider more likely, let alone the fast ones.

r001.rationale: It says short timelines still deserve attention despite being unlikely, using a few-percent chance of a world-changing event as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It does not connect incremental improvements to existing architectures with potentially explosive AI capability growth.

r003.rationale: It does not mention the possibility that advanced AI has already been developed secretly without Toby Ord's knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between saying it’s possible and saying it’s likely. I don’t think we can confidently rule out very rapid progress, but the claim that advanced AI will arrive within months is much stronger—and it matters enormously what we mean by “advanced.” A system that does remarkably well on particular tasks isn’t necessarily one that can reliably carry out a wide range of difficult projects.

The practical question is how to act under that uncertainty. We shouldn’t make all our preparations depend on having another decade. Some safeguards take years to develop, so even a relatively small chance of very short timelines is a reason to start now. But we should also avoid treating the most urgent scenario as though it were established fact.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid progress cannot be ruled out and that a small chance of short timelines warrants preparation, but it does not state that long timelines being plausible does little to reduce concern about short timelines.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss incremental improvements to existing architectures or explosive growth in AI capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that Toby Ord cannot rule out advanced AI having already been developed secretly without his knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between thinking that it’s possible and thinking that it’s likely. I wouldn’t rule out very rapid progress, but I’d be cautious about confidently predicting that advanced AI will arrive within months. There’s a lot of uncertainty both about the capabilities we’ll see and about what we mean by “advanced AI.”

For me, the practical question is how to act under that uncertainty. If there’s a credible possibility that systems with very consequential capabilities could arrive soon, then we need preparations that can work on that timescale. But we should also pursue the longer-term work, because it could take much longer. We shouldn’t make our entire response depend on one particular forecast.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges uncertainty and says to prepare for a credible near-term possibility, but does not state that plausible long timelines do little to reduce concern about short timelines.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss incremental improvements to existing architectures or explosive capability growth.

r003.rationale: It does not say that advanced AI may already have been developed behind closed doors without Toby Ord’s knowledge.
